opus-5.5.text:
I think it comes down to what agents actually demand from a model. When you move from chat to agentic work, the context explodes. The model reads files, calls tools, gets results back, reflects, tries again. You're quickly dealing with very long contexts, often tens or hundreds of thousands of tokens, and many turns of interaction. In that setting, the cost of full attention, which grows quadratically with length, and the size of the KV cache become real bottlenecks. They aren't just theoretical concerns. They decide whether you can run many rollouts in RL, whether inference is cheap enough to deploy, and how fast the agent responds.

Hybrid attention is attractive because it's a pragmatic compromise. You keep a few full attention layers so the model can still do precise retrieval over long distances, which agents really need when they have to recall an exact detail from a tool output many steps earlier. Most layers use something cheaper, like sliding window or linear attention, which handles local patterns efficiently. You get most of the capability at a fraction of the memory and compute.

There's also a deeper reason why I prefer simplicity. Each additional piece of architectural complexity is something you have to debug, optimize at the kernel level, keep stable during large-scale training, and keep consistent between training and inference. For agents in particular, so much of the capability comes from post-training and reinforcement learning, from the environments and the data, not from clever architectural tricks. If the architecture is simple and efficient, you can spend your compute on more rollouts, longer horizons, and more iterations. In my experience, that tends to matter more than a marginal gain from a more exotic design.

So my philosophy is to make the architecture just good enough and very efficient, then let scale, data, and RL do the heavy lifting. A simple architecture that you can train and serve well usually beats a sophisticated one that fights you at every step.

r001.rationale: The response says simpler architectures let compute go toward rollouts, longer horizons, and RL iterations, but does not state that they leave more room to adapt to different scenarios later.

r002.rationale: The response describes using some full-attention layers and mostly cheaper attention, but does not say their ratio can be adjusted in an already trained model.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the preference comes from being burned by the opposite. When you're serving agents, the model isn't answering one question and leaving. It's running for hundreds of steps, carrying a very long context, calling tools, reading the results back in, and doing that over and over. So the thing that kills you isn't peak capability on a benchmark, it's the cost of every incremental step as the context grows.

Full attention is beautiful, but its cost scales with context length on every single token you generate, and the KV cache grows with it. For an agent that's at two hundred thousand tokens of accumulated trajectory, that's where your latency and memory go. With a hybrid design, where most layers use linear attention or a sliding window and only a few layers keep full attention, you get something close to constant cost per step, and the KV cache stays small. The few global layers are enough to retrieve the precise things you need, like a function signature from forty steps ago. In our experiments, the quality gap was much smaller than people assumed, especially once you train it that way from the start instead of retrofitting.

The second reason is more philosophical. I think a lot of the "cleverness" in architecture ends up being a liability at scale. Every special component is something you have to make work with your parallelism strategy, your inference engine, your quantization, your RL infrastructure. For agent training in particular, you're doing massive amounts of rollouts, and if the architecture is awkward to serve, your RL loop becomes slow and your researchers iterate less. A simpler, more uniform architecture means the whole system, training and serving, is easier to reason about and optimize. That compounds.

And the third thing is that for agents, I believe more of the intelligence should come from the training signal, from the environments and the reward, rather than from architectural priors. The architecture just needs to be efficient enough to let the model experience a lot of long interactions. If I had to choose between a fancier architecture and ten times more agent trajectories at the same compute, I'd take the trajectories every time.

So it's not that I think hybrid attention is the final answer. It's that I want the architecture to get out of the way, so the real problem, which is teaching the model to act well over long horizons, gets all the attention, no pun intended.

r001.rationale: It says simpler architectures are easier to optimize and let training signals drive agent behavior, but does not say they leave more room for later adaptation to different scenarios.

r002.rationale: It describes a hybrid with mostly linear or sliding-window layers and a few full-attention layers, but does not say their ratio can be adjusted in an already trained model.

astra-6.text:
I favor simpler architectures because agents already introduce a lot of complexity at the system level. They have to reason over long histories, use tools, and interact with an environment. If the model architecture is also very complicated, it becomes harder to understand where improvements or failures come from.

Hybrid attention is an appealing compromise. You can use more efficient attention for much of the computation while retaining full attention where access to the broader context matters. The question is whether that balance preserves the capabilities an agent needs while reducing the cost of long interactions.

For me, simplicity isn’t an end in itself. I want an architecture that is easier to train, scale, and improve. If a more complicated design delivers a clear, reliable benefit, that’s a reason to use it. But the complexity should earn its place.

sol-6.1.text:
For agents, I think the architecture should serve the whole system. An agent may take many steps, use tools, and accumulate a long context. So we need to care about the cost and latency of completing a task, not just the quality of a single response.

Hybrid attention is appealing because you don’t necessarily need full attention everywhere to preserve the capabilities you care about. If a simpler design gives us a good balance of quality, memory use, and speed, we have more room for longer interactions and more experimentation.

But simplicity itself isn’t the goal. I would judge the architecture by whether the agent can reliably finish real tasks. If a more complex design delivers a meaningful improvement there, then the complexity may be justified.
